stem.text: The function f is continuous for all real x and differentiable for all x except \( x = \frac{19}{2} \), where its graph has a corner. Selected values of f are given in the table. Does the Mean Value Theorem guarantee a value c, with \( 8 < c < 11 \), such that \( f'(c) = - \frac{8}{3} \)? Justify the answer.

answer_key.label: No. Although \( \frac{f(11) - f(8)}{11 - 8} = - \frac{8}{3} \), f is not differentiable at \( x = \frac{19}{2} \), which lies in \( (8, 11) \), so the Mean Value Theorem does not apply and such a c is not guaranteed.

worked_solution.text: The average rate of change of f over \( \left[8, 11\right] \) is \( \frac{f(11) - f(8)}{11 - 8} = \frac{-3 - 5}{3} = - \frac{8}{3} \).

The Mean Value Theorem needs f continuous on \( \left[8, 11\right] \) and differentiable on \( (8, 11) \), but f is not differentiable at \( x = \frac{19}{2} \), which lies in \( (8, 11) \). The theorem does not apply, and no other fact given forces \( f'(c) = - \frac{8}{3} \) anywhere in the interval, so the answer is no.
worked_solution.rule_named: hypotheses of the Mean Value Theorem

options.label: Yes. Since \( \frac{f(11) - f(8)}{11 - 8} = - \frac{8}{3} \), there is a c with \( 8 < c < 11 \) and \( f'(c) = - \frac{8}{3} \), because an average rate of change is always reached by the derivative.
options.derivation: existence asserted from the arithmetic alone, with no theorem named and no check that one applies
